subjective.unit: Chief Complaint: Headaches for a few months
subjective.citation_text: Doctor: Hello. Could you tell me your age and gender, and what brings you in today? Patient: I'm 52 years old, and I'm a male. I'm here because I've been having these headaches for a few months, and it turns out there's a mass on my pituitary gland. Doctor: When was the pituitary mass discovered, and what was the size of the mass? Have you experienced any vision changes, hormonal imbalances, or fatigue associated with the mass or headaches? Patient: The mass was discovered a few months ago when I was being checked for the headaches. I didn't know about it until my doctor told me. I haven't had any hormonal issues or fatigue, but I have been bumping into door frames, which I guess is because of my vision. I didn't realize I had a vision problem until the doctor tested me. Doctor: Could you provide details about the size and location of the pituitary mass, as well as any prior medical evaluations or treatments related to it? Patient: The doctor mentioned that the mass is pressing on the optic chiasm, and it was discovered during an MRI. I don’t know the exact size, but it’s significant enough to cause vision issues. I haven’t had any other treatments for it yet, just the initial tests. Doctor: Could you provide the exact size of the pituitary mass as measured on the MRI, and have you undergone any visual field testing or hormonal assessments such as blood tests for pituitary hormones? Patient: I don’t know the exact size of the mass, but the doctor said it’s significant enough to be pressing on the optic chiasm. I haven’t had any visual field testing yet, but I did have blood tests for pituitary hormones, and my TSH was low, though everything else was normal. Doctor: Could you please describe the nature and frequency of your headaches, and have you noticed any other neurological symptoms such as double vision, difficulty with balance, or changes in your sense of smell? Patient: The headaches are located

reference_so.subjective:
Basic information: 52-year-old male presenting with headaches and a pituitary mass

History of present illness: Headaches for a few months, with a pituitary mass discovered. The patient reports bumping into door frames, suggesting possible visual field deficits. No hormonal imbalances or fatigue reported. The mass was discovered during an MRI and is pressing on the optic chiasm. The patient hasn’t had any other treatments for it yet, just the initial tests. Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull, nagging ache, worsening over the past few months from a 3 out of 10 to a 6 out of 10, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. The patient has not noticed changes in peripheral vision but has been bumping into door frames, which the doctor attributed to vision loss. The patient has not noticed changes in his sense of smell, and he has not had double vision or balance issues. The patient has been diagnosed with bitemporal hemianopia, as confirmed by the neurological examination, and visual field testing is pending.

Past history: No relevant past medical history, no prior surgeries, no known allergies. Family history is unremarkable for similar conditions.
reference_so.objective:
Physical examination: Vital signs are within normal limits. Neurological examination reveals no focal deficits, but the patient reports bumping into door frames, suggesting possible bitemporal hemianopia. Cranial nerve examination shows no other abnormalities.

Investigations: MRI of the brain with contrast showed a pituitary mass compressing the optic chiasm. Pituitary hormone blood tests revealed low TSH, with other hormones within normal limits. Visual field testing is pending and scheduled before surgery. Exact dimensions of the pituitary mass are not available to the patient, but it is described as significant enough to compress the optic chiasm.
